title: ‘I Came as a Jury Member, but Became a Student of Cinema’: Aanand L Rai on the Golden Peacock Jury Experience at 57th IFFI
subtitle:
Filmmakers must remain responsive to changes in cinematic grammar, irrespective of the language in which they work: Aanand L Rai, Jury Chairperson, International Competition, at 57th IFFI

Deliberations on Award Selection Were Organic, Decisions Unanimous: IFFI International Competition Jury
content:
Goa, 27 November 2026
International Jury Chairperson and Indian filmmaker Aanand L Rai, along with fellow jury members, addressed a press conference organised by the Press Information Bureau (PIB) in Goa today on the sidelines of the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI). Reflecting on their experience of evaluating 15 feature films competing for the Golden Peacock Award, the jury members spoke about the diversity of cinematic voices, the exchange of cultural perspectives and the evolving language of cinema.
Describing the experience as an opportunity to learn, Rai said that watching films from different countries and cultures, followed by discussions among jury members, offered insights into the creative choices and cultural contexts behind each work. “I came as a jury member, but while watching the films I became a student of cinema,” he said.
Explaining the jury's deliberations, Rai said the selection process was shaped by open and candid discussions, without any predetermined approach or consideration of the countries of origin of the films. He described the process as organic, with members freely sharing their responses and perspectives. “Actually, it went very organic for me. I really don't know how to put it, but we just spoke our hearts out, that's it,” he said. He added that the discussions were healthy and enriching, with members often finding common ground while bringing different perspectives to the same cinematic moments.
Emphasising that cinema is a constantly evolving art form, Rai said filmmakers must remain responsive to changes in cinematic grammar, irrespective of the language in which they work. “A film is an experience, an experience of an emotion or expression of it. Each film should do something to you. You would not be the same after watching it; it should change something within you.” he said. He added that cinematic grammar was ultimately shaped by filmmakers rather than languages.
Thai filmmaker Ratchapoom Boonbunchachoke, who returned to IFFI after his film was screened as the closing film at the previous edition, highlighted how the diverse backgrounds of jury members enriched their discussions. He said the emotional impact of a film mattered more than technical brilliance alone. “It matters how the filmmaker used the technique to emotionally impact the audience
,
” he observed.
Colombian sound designer María Alejandra Rojas described the experience as particularly meaningful from the perspective of a professional working in post-production. She said the deliberations were intellectually stimulating, with even the moments of silence following screenings adding depth to the discussions.
Argentinian filmmaker and screenwriter Sol Berruezo Pichon-Rivière appreciated the plurality of voices represented in the festival's selection. She noted that IFFI offered a platform to films from diverse countries, cultures and production scales, including works that may not have featured prominently in major international festival circuits.
Romanian writer-director and producer Bogdan Mureșanu described the overall selection as unusually strong and noted the remarkable convergence of tastes among jury members from different parts of the world. Recalling their discussions after screenings, he said, “We talked immediately after each film about what we liked or what we disliked. We were still immersed in the stories and we had this pleasure to be there a bit more till we jumped to another journey.” He also highlighted the value of listening to fellow jury members and discovering different perspectives on the films.
The jury members' reflections underscored the role of international film festivals in bringing diverse cinematic traditions into conversation and creating opportunities for shared learning and appreciation.
The press conference was moderated by Shri Rajith Chandran.

title: ‘The Villain Is Not Always an Individual, but a Reflection of Society’: Karthik Subbaraj at 57th IFFI
subtitle: Filmmaker explores morality, patriarchy and cinema’s potential to challenge social prejudices
content:
Goa, 27 November 2026
Renowned filmmaker Karthik Subbaraj explored the complexities of morality, the societal roots of villainy and cinema’s potential to challenge prejudice during an interview session titled “
What If the Villain Is Right?”
at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa. Moderated by film critic Sudhir Srinivasan, the session examined how his films challenge conventional distinctions between good and evil.
Observing that human behaviour is shaped by circumstances and social experiences, Subbaraj said, “
The base is grey for everyone
.” He explained that the people individuals encounter and the situations they experience influence how they are perceived as good or bad.
Discussing his film
Dorothy
, Subbaraj distinguished between characters who consciously commit evil and those whose harmful behaviour stems from deeply ingrained social conditioning. While Whistle Veeraiya represents an overtly evil character, he suggested that figures such as the parotta shop owner could be more dangerous because they fail to recognise their own prejudices and wrongdoing.
Subbaraj said
Dorothy
portrays masculinity and patriarchal attitudes as the forces behind the protagonist’s death, positioning an oppressive mindset, rather than a single individual, as the real antagonist. Drawing a parallel with
Mercury
, he explained how the collective mentality of a village is portrayed negatively, showing how individual acts of villainy can emerge from wider social attitudes.
Reflecting on humiliation and accountability, the filmmaker observed that ridicule and laughter directed at someone's inability can be more hurtful than reprimand. He also spoke about remorse and guilt as forms of punishment, noting that the consequences of one's actions need not always take the form of physical harm or death.
On cinema's ability to influence society, Subbaraj recalled audience responses to
Dorothy
, including moments when viewers embraced transgender people and men were moved to tears. Such reactions, he said, reinforced his belief that films can go beyond entertainment to foster empathy and encourage social change. He added that the idea of bringing about change through storytelling had also informed his approach to
Jigarthanda
.
Throughout the conversation, Subbaraj emphasised his reluctance to portray characters as entirely virtuous heroes or irredeemably evil villains. By leaving moral judgments open to interpretation, he invites audiences to examine characters and their motivations from their own perspectives.
The session offered insights into Subbaraj’s cinematic approach, in which villainy is often rooted not merely in individuals, but in the social attitudes and structures that shape them.
Subbaraj’s reflections underscored cinema’s ability to look beyond conventional notions of good and evil, encouraging audiences to question ingrained prejudices and engage with complex social realities. Resonating with the theme of the 57th International Film Festival of India, ‘Stories Without Borders’, his approach to storytelling highlights how narratives rooted in specific social and cultural contexts can raise universal questions about morality, empathy and human behaviour.

title: Filmmakers Share the Creative Journeys behind The Kerala Story 2 : Goes Beyond and Demography Is Destiny at IFFI 2026
content:
Goa, 27 November 2026
The importance of character-driven narratives, research-based filmmaking and the power of cinema to bring diverse stories to audiences came into focus at a press conference held on the sidelines of the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) today. Director Kamakhya Narayan Singh and producer Ravindra Sanghavi shared insights into the making of
The Kerala Story 2 : Goes Beyond
and the documentary
Demography Is Destiny
, discussing research, character development and the challenges of presenting complex subjects through cinema.
Sharing his experience of directing
The Kerala Story 2
, Kamakhya Narayan described the film as a character-driven narrative, noting that bringing together multiple stories while maintaining a common emotional thread was both a challenge and a rewarding experience. He highlighted the role of music in connecting the different narratives, explaining that despite the film exploring three separate stories, a shared emotional core helped bind them together.
Narayan also said that the film draws upon case studies and factual references, with the intention of presenting its narrative through the experiences and emotions of its characters.
Speaking about
Demography Is Destiny
, producer Ravindra Sanghavi and director Kamakhya Narayan highlighted the challenges of translating empirical data into an engaging cinematic narrative. Kamakhya explained that finding relatable characters is essential to making complex information accessible to audiences. Drawing on his experience as a documentary filmmaker, Kamakhya said his process generally begins with data collection and interviews, followed by identifying individuals whose experiences can help shape the narrative.
He also spoke about the importance of visual authenticity in filmmaking, including selecting locations that lend credibility to the story. His travel experiences and familiarity with different places helped him identify suitable locations, to recreate the desired visual setting.
The speakers also reflected on the role of social media in helping films reach wider audiences, while emphasising that their respective creative journeys were driven by the desire to tell stories they considered meaningful.
The discussion also turned to the role of IFFI in providing a platform for films from different regions, languages and production backgrounds. Singh observed that the festival enables filmmakers working with varied budgets and resources to present their work on the same platform. He recalled how IFFI had introduced him to international cinema and filmmakers early in his career, well before digital streaming platforms became widely available.
Singh described the festival's theme, ‘Stories Without Borders’, as closely aligned with its long-standing role in bringing diverse cinematic voices together. The platform, he said, allows films from smaller regions and lesser-known languages to reach wider audiences.

title: Portuguese Film ‘Come With Me’ Explores Friendship and the Shared Experience of Cinema at 57th IFFI
subtitle: Filmmakers discuss the enduring appeal of theatrical viewing, universal themes and the evolving relationship between art-house and mainstream cinema
content:
Goa, 27 November 2026
Director João Lameira, actor António Simão and producer Daniel Pereira addressed a press conference organised by the Press Information Bureau (PIB) in Goa today on the sidelines of the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI), following the World Premiere of their Portuguese film
Come with Me (Anda daí)
, featured in the Cinema of the World section. The filmmakers discussed the film’s themes of friendship, its art-house sensibility and the continuing relevance of the theatrical experience amid the growth of streaming platforms.
Emphasising the importance of watching films together, actor António Simão expressed concern over declining cinema audiences in Portugal and the growing preference for watching films at home. He said cinema-going was also about meeting people and sharing a collective cultural experience. “
People need to be together and talk and see each other
,” he said, adding, “Long live cinema.”
Producer Daniel Pereira reaffirmed his commitment to theatrical exhibition, noting that his production and distribution company continues to prioritise cinema releases. While acknowledging the influence of streaming platforms, he viewed them as complementary to, rather than a replacement for, the theatrical experience.
Speaking about the film, director João Lameira said that although its story is rooted in Lisbon and its cultural setting, its central theme of male friendship is intended to resonate with audiences across geographical and cultural boundaries. “
I hope the story and the characters are universal enough to be understood by everyone
,” he said, adding that the specificity of the setting and characters could itself help audiences connect with the story.
Lameira also clarified that he had not approached the film with a particular classification, such as art-house or mainstream cinema, in mind. His intention was to make the film he wanted to make while hoping that audiences would appreciate it. Pereira observed that the distinction between art-house and mainstream cinema had evolved over time, noting that films with distinctive directorial perspectives and compelling stories were once more accessible to wider audiences.
Reflecting on his approach to acting, Simão spoke about how personal experiences, observation and imagination shape a performance. Drawing on his extensive theatre background, he said the character initially felt close to his own life, making him conscious of the personal experiences he might bring to the role. He eventually moved beyond these concerns to focus on the character’s circumstances and actions.
The filmmakers also expressed their appreciation for presenting the film’s World Premiere at IFFI. Acknowledging the historical and architectural connections between Portugal and Goa, they said that while some aspects of the region felt familiar, the overall experience remained culturally distinct. They welcomed the opportunity to explore Goa and share their work with Indian audiences.
The press conference was moderated by Smt. Vishali P.

title: Virtual Bharat Explores India’s Diverse Storytelling Traditions and the Global Power of Indian Cinema at IFFI 2026

content:
Goa, 27 November 2026
A panel discussion on
Virtual Bharat
explored India’s diverse storytelling traditions, creative freedom and the evolving landscape of cinema on the sidelines of the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) today. The session featured Bharat Bala, acclaimed filmmaker and Dhiraj Singh, an Indian Information Service (IIS) officer currently serving as Vice Chancellor of the Film and Television Institute of India (FTII), Pune and Managing Director (Additional Charge), National Film Development Corporation (NFDC).
Vani Tripathi Tikoo, actor, producer, theatre practitioner and cultural leader, conceptualised and moderated the session.
The engaging discussion explored the importance of authentic grassroots narratives and India's growing presence in international cinema, with Vani Tripathi Tikoo sharing her perspectives and bringing depth and direction to the conversation.
‘Filmmakers must first recognise and bring forth the stories within their own country’
Speaking about his creative philosophy, Bala said he did not differentiate between music videos, short films, feature films, fiction and non-fiction, emphasising that storytelling and creative expression must remain central to every format.
Reflecting on his work over the past five years, he spoke about taking cameras to the remotest corners of the country, engaging with real people, building their trust and providing them with a platform to share their own stories. He emphasised that the essence of filmmaking lies in capturing authentic human experiences rather than imposing preconceived narratives.
Highlighting the Virtual Bharat initiative, which brings together 143 films on a cloud-based platform, Bala underscored India’s extraordinary cultural and geographical diversity as an immense source of untold stories. He observed that filmmakers must first recognise and bring forth the stories within their own country to establish a meaningful global presence. “Bharat is the new global,” he remarked, emphasising that authentic narratives rooted in India’s lived experiences can resonate with audiences across the world.
‘Artistic expression draws its strength from human experiences’
Noting that the country possesses a vast audience base and an extraordinary reservoir of stories, Dhiraj Singh reflected on India’s potential to emerge as a stronger voice in global storytelling. He stressed the need for Indian cinema to draw from its own cultural ethos rather than remain confined by external perceptions and influences. Reflecting on the relationship between cinema, art and reality, he observed that artistic expression draws its strength from human experiences and eventually creates its own world.
Singh said the purpose of Film Festivals extends beyond screening films. Festivals, he noted, introduce audiences to the wider world of cinema, nurture cinematic appreciation and provide emerging filmmakers with opportunities to learn, interact and showcase their work. He also highlighted IFFI’s initiatives to engage young talent, including students from the Film and Television Institute of India (FTII), Pune, and the Film and Television Institute (FTI), Arunachal Pradesh. Providing students with exposure, creative opportunities and a platform to engage with the cinematic community, he said, was an important aspect of film education.
The discussion also addressed the growing influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on the creative industries. Responding to concerns about AI replacing creative professionals, Singh said that rather than being apprehensive, creators must remain alert to technological developments and undertake timely course corrections. He emphasised that human creativity and artistic expression cannot be replaced, as art ultimately emerges from human imagination and experience.
Bala welcomed AI as an evolving technology that could expand creative possibilities and open new avenues for filmmakers. However, he maintained that storytelling remains fundamentally rooted in human creativity and originality. He said technological advancements should encourage creators to become more innovative and push the boundaries of original storytelling.
The discussion highlighted the growing importance of platforms such as Virtual Bharat in bringing India’s diverse and authentic stories to the forefront, while reaffirming the role of film festivals in nurturing talent, encouraging creative exchange and strengthening India’s presence on the global cinematic stage.

title: Revisiting 2001: Filmmakers Who Took Hindi Cinema in New Directions Reunite 25 Years Later
subtitle:
“Cinema Is a Mirror to Society; I Believe in Exploring Real Life Rather Than Reel Life”: Madhur Bhandarkar

“How an actor listens and reacts to a cue is very important”: Ashutosh Gowariker

“Be Fearless, Leave Your Ego Behind and Tell Your Own Story”: Farhan Akhtar on the Art of Filmmaking
content:
Goa, 27 November 2026
A village takes on an empire with a game of cricket. Three friends navigate friendship, heartbreak and the uncertainties of growing up. And a filmmaker turns the camera towards women and realities society often chooses to ignore. Three films with unconventional stories, 2001 was one of the most remarkable years in Hindi cinema.
Lagaan
,
Dil Chahta Hai
and
Chandni Bar
didn't just entertain; they challenged conventions, broke new ground and changed the cinematic conversation. While
Lagaan
celebrated the spirit of rebellion,
Dil Chahta Hai
captured the mood of a generation, and
Chandni Bar
brought attention to women and lives often left unseen.
Twenty-five years later, the creative mavericks behind these iconic films—Ashutosh Gowariker, Farhan Akhtar and Madhur Bhandarkar reunited at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI), Goa, for ‘The Legendary 25s’, a session that celebrated films that dared to break the mould and creators who chose to follow their own path.
“AI May Change Filmmaking, But It Cannot Replace the Human Soul”
Championing cinema as a reflection of society, filmmaker Madhur Bhandarkar reiterated his commitment to telling stories drawn from real life, particularly those that bring untold narratives and overlooked realities to the forefront. Recalling the challenges of advocating for female-centric subjects at a time when the industry was hesitant to embrace unconventional portrayals of women, he spoke about how films like
Chandni Bar
,
Corporate
and
Fashion
emerged from his conviction to portray women in all their complexities, vulnerabilities and strengths. “I have always wanted to make films about subjects that people hesitate to talk about or even explore. I am drawn to the stories behind the scenes, the realities that often remain hidden from the public eye. For me, cinema has always been a mirror to society. I would rather explore real life than create an idealised reel life,” he said.
Emphasising the importance of creative courage and conviction, Bhandarkar urged filmmakers to remain true to the stories they believe in rather than be influenced by prevailing industry trends or audience expectations. He also reflected on the growing role of technology in filmmaking, acknowledging that AI and visual effects could open up exciting new dimensions in visual storytelling. However, he firmly maintained that technology could never replace the human element that gives cinema its emotional depth.
“AI and VFX can certainly enhance the visual experience and expand the possibilities of filmmaking, but they can never replace the human touch. Technology can create images, but it cannot replicate human emotions, sensitivity and the emotional connect that breathe life into a character,” he added.
“Every Film Is a Reset to Zero. The Magic of Acting Lies in the Silence Between Words.”
Reflecting on his creative journey, Ashutosh Gowariker described every new film as a “reset to zero”, requiring a fresh perspective, an open mind and the willingness to rediscover the art of storytelling. Highlighting the challenges faced by unconventional cinema, he said, “Anything that is new, different or unconventional needs more time to find its audience. We must not judge a film only by its opening weekend.”
Sharing his insights into the craft of acting, he emphasised the importance of listening, expressions and pauses in bringing a character to life. “For me, a true performance lies in the pauses. Listening is one of the most important qualities of an actor. How an actor listens and reacts to a cue is equally important,” he said.
Reiterating that filmmakers should trust their stories rather than presume what audiences want, he stressed the importance of allowing viewers to form their own interpretations.
“Tell Your Story Fearlessly. Leave Your Ego at the Door.”
Championing originality and creative fearlessness, Farhan Akhtar urged aspiring filmmakers to trust their instincts and tell stories that reflect their own vision. Emphasising the importance of breaking away from conventional thinking, he said, “A director or writer must keep an open heart and mind, and leave their ego behind. Be fearless, believe in your vision and tell the story you truly want to tell.”
Describing a screenplay as a “living, breathing thing”, Farhan highlighted how a story evolves through the collective imagination of writers, actors and technicians. He stressed that filmmaking is a collaborative process, where setting aside individual egos allows a story to grow and find its true voice. He also cautioned against letting excessive promotions overshadow the essence of cinema, emphasising that meaningful storytelling and a genuine audience connect should always come first.
As the conversation drew to a close, one thought stood out: great cinema is born out of creative courage, original storytelling and the willingness to challenge conventions. Twenty-five years after Lagaan, Dil Chahta Hai and Chandni Bar explored different facets of Indian society and reshaped the cinematic conversation, their creators reaffirmed the enduring power of stories rooted in human experiences.
Echoing the spirit of the 57th International Film Festival of India, under the theme ‘Stories Without Borders’, the discussion highlighted how authentic stories, irrespective of their cultural or geographical origins, can transcend boundaries and resonate with audiences everywhere. As technology continues to transform filmmaking, it is ultimately human emotions, creative conviction and the universality of storytelling that give cinema its enduring appeal.
The session was moderated by acclaimed actor and producer Khushboo Sundar.

title: ‘Paro: The Untold Story of Bride Slavery’ Explores the Plight of Women Caught in the Web of Bride Trafficking
subtitle: Actor-Producer and Screenplay writer Trupti Bhoir brings a hard-hitting story of exploitation, gender inequality and women’s rights to the 57th IFFI
content:
Goa, 27 November 2026
Paro: The Untold Story of Bride Slavery
, featured in the Indian Panorama section of the 57th  International Film Festival of India (IFFI), brings to light the disturbing and largely under-reported practice of buying and selling women as brides, particularly in Mewat, Haryana. The term ‘Paro’ is used in the region to refer to women who are bought or sold into marriage.
Speaking in a press conference, actor and producer Trupti Bhoir shared that, she has undertaken 4.5 years of research to make this film, which is her second Oscar-listed film. In an unusual creative journey in this film, Trupti Bhoir has taken on the triple responsibility of producer, screenplay writer and protagonist.
A challenging research that led to making of the film
The idea for the film emerged from Trupti Bhoir’s exposure to documentaries and media reports highlighting the practice of bride slavery in India. Known for films centred on women’s issues and rights, she was deeply disturbed by the realities she encountered.
With the help of an NGO, Bhoir and her mother visited the villages disguised as journalists. They met around 62–63 women subjected to bride slavery, hailing from Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Gujarat and Delhi.
Bhoir remarked that the bride trade is rooted in gender inequality and poverty. It is not confined to Haryana but is a wider national concern, with women and girls from several states falling victim to the practice.
One of the most disturbing accounts uncovered during the research was that of a girl aged approximately 11–13 years, who had reportedly been sold for a meager amount. This young girl's story became the inspiration for the protagonist of the film, a character portrayed by Trupti Bhoir herself. Through this character, the filmmaker seeks to bring to the screen the pain, helplessness and brutal exploitation experienced by countless women whose stories often remain unheard.
Taking the fight beyond cinema
The film's significance extends beyond storytelling. Trupti Bhoir said that NGO Shelter Foundation has compiled data on approximately 2,000 women who are victims of bride slavery. The data was submitted to the Chairperson of the National Commission for Women, Vijaya Rahatkar, around a year and three months ago. A fact-finding committee has subsequently been constituted by the Union Government. “I salute the Government which has taken steps to address this issue. This is another reason for me to make this film,” she said.
Trafficking of women: A global issue
Bhoir also pointed out that missing girls and sexual violence are concerns across the world. While awareness about human trafficking and prostitution has increased significantly over the last 15–20 years, the buying and selling of brides and the practice of bride slavery continue to receive comparatively little attention. Her interactions during screenings at film festivals and institutions across the world have reinforced her belief that this issue needs greater international awareness and discussion.
With ‘
Paro: The Untold Story of Bride Slavery
’, Trupti Bhoir hopes to take a deeply disturbing social issue from the margins to the mainstream and initiate conversations about gender inequality, bride slavery and the dignity and rights of women.
The press conference was moderated by Shubhankar Vashisth.

content:
Goa, 27 November 2026
Cinema is a universal language, one that brings people together through stories, emotions and experiences.
While many experience the magic of cinema through striking frames and unspoken emotions, true inclusivity lies in bringing these unseen moments to life for every member of the audience.
Taking this spirit of inclusivity forward, the Indian Panorama section of the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) 2026 is extending the cinematic experience to audiences with diverse accessibility needs.
In collaboration with
Cinedubs
, the initiative is facilitating Audio Description (AD) and Closed Captions (CC) for 25 selected feature films being screened at INOX-2, enabling persons with visual and hearing impairments to engage with the stories in an interesting and meaningful way. This initiative forms part of IFFI's broader efforts to make the festival experience more inclusive for audiences with diverse accessibility needs
The 57th IFFI proudly champions
Sabka Manoranjan
(Entertainment for All), pushing the boundaries to create a festival that celebrates diversity, accessibility, and inclusivity. To capitalise on this vision, the Cinedubs mobile application is allowing audiences to access Audio Description and Closed Captions on their personal smartphones, using headphones during film screenings, making cinema a truly shared experience, accessible to all cinema enthusiasts.
Bridging the gap, Audio Description offers narration of key visual details, including actions, settings, facial expressions and other elements that may not be conveyed through dialogue. Meanwhile, bringing the auditory experience to the screen through textual representation of dialogues, sound effects and other relevant audio cues, Closed Captions are making films more accessible to persons with hearing impairments.
These features work alongside the regular screening, enabling viewers to follow the film in real time without interrupting the shared cinematic experience. title: Smart Boards vs. Blackboards: ‘Kabir Sir Ka Akhri Lesson’ Strikes an Emotional Chord at IFFI
subtitle: Filmmaker reflects on the changing relationship between teachers and students in the age of technology
content:
Goa, 27 November 2026
What happens when teachers who once shaped generations find themselves struggling to keep pace with changing classrooms? This question lies at the heart of
Kabir Sir Ka Akhri Lesson
, the debut Hindi feature film by filmmaker Sarfaraz Alam, which had its World Premiere at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI).
The film draws inspiration from an experience that Alam encountered during a visit to his childhood school in Bihar's Nalanda district. He found that traditional blackboards had given way to smart boards, while veteran teachers were struggling to adapt to the new technologies. What he witnessed prompted him to reflect on the changing realities of the teaching profession and the challenges faced by educators today.
Recalling the experience during a press conference organised by the Press Information Bureau (PIB) in Goa today, Alam said, “Two years ago, when I visited my school, I saw my teachers struggling with new technologies as smart boards replaced the blackboard. That is how the idea came in.”
Tracing his journey from a modest village school in Bihar to studying medicine in Russia and subsequently pursuing filmmaking at the New York Film Academy, Alam spoke about the lasting influence of his teachers and the connection he continues to share with his roots. He observed that educators who once guided generations of doctors, engineers and IAS officers are today navigating technological barriers and changing attitudes towards the teaching profession. “This movie is based on what they are facing today and how they are treated. It will connect with audiences across the entire country,” he said.
Produced by Kartina Entertainment and Sports Private Limited, the 103.52-minute Hindi drama features acclaimed actor Vinay Pathak in the lead role. Alam praised Pathak's performance and also reflected on the changing dynamics between teachers, students and parents. He noted that the close emotional bond that once characterised teacher-student relationships is increasingly missing from modern education. Emphasising the importance of thoughtful communication, he urged young people to observe and listen carefully rather than speak ill of others.
Speaking about Bihar, Alam highlighted the state's infrastructural progress and underscored the role of cinema in bringing its development and achievements to wider audiences.
Beyond the transition from blackboards to smart boards,
Kabir Sir Ka Akhri Lesson
raises questions about respect, changing generations and the place of teachers in an evolving society. Its story, rooted in a filmmaker's personal experience, touches upon a universal relationship that transcends geographical and cultural boundaries. This resonates with the theme of the 57th IFFI, being held in Goa from November 20 to 28, 2026: ‘Stories Without Borders’.
The press conference was moderated by Shri Vivek Vishwas.

title: Building a Home Away from Home: ‘Paris Paris’ Explores Displacement, Identity and Belonging
subtitle: Belgian filmmaker Isabelle Tollenaere discusses migration and the universal search for a place to call home, at IFFI 2026
content:
Goa, 27 November 2026
Belgian filmmaker Isabelle Tollenaere shared insights into her film
Paris Paris
, its creative journey and the themes of migration, displacement and belonging at a press conference organised by the Press Information Bureau (PIB) during the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa today. Featured in the International Cinema category, the film explores the meaning of home through the lives of three men living in the French capital.
Set in a building in Paris,
Paris Paris
follows three men from different backgrounds as they attempt to build a home for themselves in a squatted apartment. Sharing limited resources and exchanging conversations about their past and future, the men navigate questions of identity, displacement and belonging, bringing out the human experiences that connect people across cultures.
Expressing her delight at visiting India for the first time, Tollenaere described the opportunity to present her film at IFFI as an honour. She recalled that the screening held the previous day had received an encouraging response, with the auditorium filled to capacity. The engaging question-and-answer session that followed provided an opportunity to interact with Indian audiences and understand their perspectives on the film.
Speaking about her creative approach, Tollenaere explained how her background in documentary filmmaking shaped her casting choices. She selected individuals whose personal histories and lived experiences resonated with those of the characters they portray, bringing authenticity and depth to the narrative.
The filmmaker also spoke about the challenges involved in the production, particularly those arising from a limited budget and the process of identifying suitable filming locations. Sharing the personal inspiration behind the film, she revealed that her grandparents were immigrants, an experience that shaped her interest in migration, displacement and the search for belonging.
Expressing her hopes for the film, Tollenaere said she would love to see it travel across countries and cultures, connecting with audiences around the world through its universal themes and shared human experiences.

title: Second Regional Conference on Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 concludes at Agra, Emphasising Sustainability, Community Ownership and Gram Panchayat-led Water Governance
subtitle:
Senior Officials Visit Water Supply Infrastructure and Participate In Jal Arpan Diwas Celebrations Across Five Villages in Uttar Pradesh

Participating States/UTs reaffirm their commitment towards accelerating implementation of Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                27 NOV 2026 6:09PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The second regional Conference on Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0,
organised by the Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation (DDWS), Ministry of Jal Shakti, Government of India, concluded today at Agra, Uttar Pradesh. The conference brought together representatives of seven northern States and Union Territories to deliberate on key strategies for accelerating implementation, strengthening sustainability and ensuring long-term functionality of rural drinking water supply systems
As part of the two-day regional conference, Shri Ashok K. K. Meena, Secretary, Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation (DDWS), Ministry of Jal Shakti
, today visited rural drinking water supply infrastructure and participated in the Jal Arpan Diwas celebration at Badhera (Bhadaira) W/S Scheme and 456 MLD WTP, Etah.
In the valedictory session, Secretary, DDWS
emphasised that the Regional Conference had provided an important platform for States/UT to develop a common understanding of the reforms envisaged under Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 and to learn from one another's experiences. Referring to the field visits undertaken during the day, he highlighted innovative practices observed in Uttar Pradesh, including the use of solar energy for rural water supply schemes and command-and-control systems for monitoring and operation of water supply infrastructure, and encouraged States to examine such practices for wider replication.
Highlighting that rural drinking water service delivery is fundamentally a local service, Shri Meena stressed the importance of strengthening ownership of water supply assets by Gram Panchayats and local communities. He noted that Jal Arpan represents an important step towards transferring responsibility and ownership of drinking water infrastructure to communities and underscored the need to build the financial, technical and institutional capacities of Gram Panchayats for sustained service delivery.
He said that infrastructure creation must be complemented by effective management, regular water quality surveillance and community participation. He reiterated the need for convergence among Departments of Panchayati Raj, Rural Development, Skill Development and Drinking Water to strengthen operation and maintenance, build local capacities and promote source sustainability through initiatives such as Jal Sanchay Jan Bhagidari. He called upon States to move towards sustainable, community-owned and efficiently managed rural drinking water systems while strengthening Gram Panchayats as the foundation of Viksit Villages and Viksit Bharat.
Shri Kamal Kishore Soan, AS&MD, NJJM
called for digital mapping of all drinking water supply infrastructure and highlighted the importance of leveraging existing institutional platforms for capacity building and strengthening Gram Panchayat-led water governance. He informed that a joint initiative has been undertaken by DDWS and the Ministry of Panchayati Raj to align training programmes under SBM-G with the existing capacity-building framework under Rashtriya Gram Swaraj Abhiyan (RGSA).
He emphasised that integrating water and sanitation-related training modules into ongoing Panchayati Raj training programmes would help strengthen the capacities of Sarpanches, Panchayat Secretaries and other grassroots functionaries. He urged States to enhance coordination with Panchayati Raj institutions and utilise existing training ecosystems to build awareness, strengthen community ownership and improve long-term management of rural drinking water supply systems.
Summarising the key outcomes of the two-day deliberations,
Shri D. Senthil Pandiyan, Joint Secretary, DDWS
, noted that ensuring sustainable rural drinking water services requires a whole-of-government approach and cannot be achieved by a single department alone. He highlighted the importance of convergence among departments dealing with drinking water, Panchayati Raj, Rural Development, Tribal Affairs and Skill Development for effective implementation of Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 reforms.
Shri Pandiyan called for working towards strengthened Gram Panchayat ownership of water supply infrastructure, capacity building of VWSCs and Sujalam Shakti, digital monitoring through the Sujalam framework, water quality surveillance, source sustainability, Jal Arpan, and institutional mechanisms for long-term operation and maintenance. He also appreciated the exchange of best practices by participating States and called upon them to undertake
timely implementation of the agreed reform measures and action plans.
During the concluding day of the conference,
Shri Vijay Kumar, Director, Ministry of Panchayati Raj
, highlighted the opportunities available under the 16th Finance Commission framework for strengthening rural drinking water service delivery and sustainability. He emphasised the importance of mapping water supply infrastructure on the e-GramSwaraj portal, integrating drinking water priorities into Gram Panchayat Development Plans and effectively utilising Finance Commission grants for operation, maintenance and management of rural water supply assets. He also encouraged States to strengthen Panchayat planning processes and maximise the benefits of performance-linked grants through improved local governance and service delivery outcomes.
Field Visits and Jal Arpan Diwas Celebrations
Five teams comprising senior officials from the Government of India, participating States and Union Territories, partner Ministries and technical institutions visited rural drinking water supply schemes and participated in Jal Arpan ceremonies across Uttar Pradesh. The visits covered the Badhera (Bhadaira) Water Supply Scheme in Etah district, Nagla Babu Water Supply Scheme in Hathras district, Simrau Water Supply Scheme in Mainpuri district, Shahpur Qutub Water Supply Scheme in Aligarh district and Sultanpur Water Supply Scheme in Hathras district.
The field visits were led by senior officials, including Ashok K K Meena, Secretary, DDWS, Shri. Kamal Kishore Soan, AS & MD, NJJM, D Senthil Paniyan, Joint Secretary, NJJM, Director and Deputy Secretary, NJJM along with representatives from SPM NIWAS and participating States/UTs. The teams observed water treatment and distribution systems, interactions with PRIs, Village Water and Sanitation Committees (VWSCs), water quality testing with FTK by trained women and community participation in operation and maintenance of drinking water infrastructure.
During the field visit to villages on the occasion of Jal Arpan Diwas,
Shri Ashok K.K.Meena, Secretary, DDWS and Shri Kamal Kishore Soan, AS&MD, NJJM drank water directly from household taps
, reinforcing community confidence in the quality and safety of the drinking water being supplied. They encouraged officials to adopt similar practices during field visits to build public trust in rural drinking water services and emphasised that Jal Arpan should be communicated as a step towards shared responsibility for sustainable water service delivery, rather than merely the handover of infrastructure. He also underscored the need to reassure Gram Panchayats of continued technical support from implementing departments, particularly for major repairs and infrastructure breakdowns, to strengthen their confidence in managing village water supply systems.
During the Jal Arpan ceremonies, Gram Panchayats, VWSC members, Self Help groups, school children and community representatives participated in activities promoting water conservation, responsible water use and community ownership of drinking water assets. The events highlighted the importance of shared responsibility among communities, Gram Panchayats and implementing agencies for ensuring sustainable rural drinking water services.
Over the two days, discussions focused on implementation of reforms, source sustainability, operation and maintenance, skilling of local human resources, inter-ministerial convergence, financial sustainability and strengthening community ownership of rural drinking water infrastructure.
The Conference concluded with participating States/UTs reaffirming their commitment towards accelerating implementation of Jal Jeevan Mission 2.0 and advancing the transition towards sustainable, community-owned and service-oriented rural drinking water systems. The insights emerging from the deliberations and field visits are expected to strengthen interstate learning, improve programme implementation and contribute to long-term water security in rural areas.

title: Union MSME Minister Shri Jitan Ram Manjhi to Inaugurate NSSH Office and Preside over National SC-ST Hub Conclave in Raipur
subtitle: Opening New Doors for SC-ST Entrepreneurs: National SC-ST Hub Conclave to be Held in Raipur
date:

                27 NOV 2026 5:41PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME), Government of India is organizing ‘National SC-ST Hub Conclave’ on 28th November, 2026, at Pandit Deendayal Upadhyay Auditorium, Raipur, Chhattisgarh. The purpose of the Conclave is to promote entrepreneurship and spread awareness about the National SC-ST Hub Scheme and other MSME initiatives and to support, encourage existing/aspiring entrepreneurs of the State.  The event will bring together major stakeholders viz. CPSEs, Banks, Financial Institutions, GeM and State Government which are working towards development of MSMEs and extend handholding support.  It will also provide a platform to interact with aspiring/existing SC/ST entrepreneurs, CPSEs, Industry Associations, lending institutions to enhance participation of SC/ST
Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs)
in public procurement.
The Conclave will be presided over by Shri Jitan Ram Manjhi, Union Minister of MSME, in the presence of Shri Guru Khushwant Saheb, Minister of Scheduled Caste Development, Skill Development, Technical Education and Employment, Govt. of Chhattisgarh and Shri Lakhan Lal Dewangan, Minister of Commerce and Industries Govt. of Chhattisgarh
. The Conclave will also be attended by  Shri Purandar Mishra, Member of Legislative Assembly and Senior officers of Central & State Governments.
The Public Procurement Policy for MSEs of Central Government, mandates that Central Ministries, Departments, and PSUs shall procure at least 25% of their annual requirements from MSEs, including 4% from SC/ST-owned MSEs and 3% from women-owned MSEs.
“National SC-ST Hub (NSSH) Scheme” was launched by Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi in October 2016 with the objective of augmenting the capacity of SC/ST entrepreneurs and to empower them to participate in public procurement process and to fulfil the mandated target of 4% public procurement from SC/ST owned MSEs. Several initiatives have been undertaken under NSSH to boost entrepreneurship among SC/STs in capacity building, market linkage, finance facilitation, tender bid participation, etc. To ease the access to latest technology, under Special Credit Linked Capital Subsidy, 25% subsidy (upto Rs. 25 lakh) is provided to SC/ST MSEs engaged in manufacturing and service Sectors for procurement of Plant & Machinery/ Equipment on institutional finance. Since inception of the Scheme in October 2016, there has been 36 fold increase in public procurement from SC/ST MSE in FY 2025-26. To further expand the outreach of the NSSH Scheme in the State of Chhattisgarh, a NSSH Office is being inaugurated at Kachna, Raipur. title: Dr. Jitendra Singh Urges GAD/ Personnel Secretaries of States and UTs to Adopt Best Governance Practices, Strengthen Administrative Reforms and Build a "role-based" Citizen-Centric governance Ecosystem
subtitle:
Union Minister addresses Annual Conference of Secretaries of Personnel and General Administration Departments of States and Union Territories at Lucknow

Minister Says Government's Administrative Reforms Since 2014 Have Focused on Removing Outdated Rules, Simplifying Procedures and Strengthening Citizens' Trust

Dr. Jitendra Singh Calls for Timely Cadre Reviews and Central Deputation, Says These Are Important for Administrative Efficiency and Officers' Career Progression

Dr. Jitendra Singh Says Civil Servants Must Be Technology-Savvy, Ethically Grounded and Effective Communicators; Urges States to Share Best Governance Practices
ministry: Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances & Pensions
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                27 NOV 2026 5:29PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science & Technology and Earth Sciences, and MoS PMO, Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, Atomic Energy and Space, Dr. Jitendra Singh, today called upon States and Union Territories to strengthen administrative reforms, promote inter-state collaboration and build a responsive, "role-based", technology-driven and citizen-centric governance ecosystem.
Addressing the Annual Conference of Secretaries (Personnel/GAD) of States and Union Territories at Lucknow, he said that the evolving governance landscape requires administrators to move beyond conventional rule-based functioning towards a role-oriented approach, with greater emphasis on institutional capacity, professional competence, ethical conduct and responsiveness to citizens.
The conference, organised by the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT), brought together Secretaries (Personnel/GAD) and senior administrative officers from various States and Union Territories to deliberate on administrative reforms, personnel management, capacity building and the exchange of successful governance practices. Chief Secretary of Uttar Pradesh Shashi Prakash Goyal; Secretary, DoPT, Rachna Shah; Secretary, Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances (DARPG), Nivedita Shukla Verma, and other senior officers and representatives from States and UTs participated in the conference.
Dr. Jitendra Singh also conveyed his appreciation to Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath and the State administration for their continued cooperation in hosting national-level administrative and capacity-building programmes in the State.
During the Conference Dr. Jitendra Singh said that the Government has consistently encouraged the practice of taking national-level conferences and governance-related deliberations beyond Delhi to different regions of the country. Recalling initiatives undertaken across the States, he said that the objective was to ensure wider administrative outreach, strengthen a sense of participation among officers and provide opportunities for direct interaction between Central and State administrations.
He cited the example of organising a North-Eastern regional conference in Itanagar instead of limiting it to Guwahati, as well as taking governance conferences to locations such as Leh and Katra. Such initiatives, he said, have helped senior Central Government officers establish direct engagement with State administrations and understand regional governance challenges more closely.
The Minister said that the approach has also strengthened the exchange of best practices between the Centre and States. Referring to the District Governance Index developed through DARPG, he appreciated Uttar Pradesh for being among the early States to adopt the initiative. He said that successful models developed at the national level should be adapted by States, while effective State-level practices should also find wider application across the country.
Referring to the governance approach adopted since 2014 under Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Dr. Jitendra Singh said the focus has been on removing outdated rules and procedures rather than merely introducing new regulations. He cited the introduction of self-attestation in place of the requirement for gazetted officers to attest documents, describing it as an important expression of the Government's trust in the youth of the country.
He also referred to the discontinuation of interviews for recruitment to several lower-level government posts and various legislative and administrative changes in the pension system. Explaining the broader approach towards pensioners' welfare, he said that reforms have extended beyond pension disbursement to address the changing needs and circumstances of beneficiaries.
The Minister cited amendments enabling separated daughters to receive family pension and allowing women employees to nominate their children, rather than being restricted to their spouse, as nominees for family pension. These changes, he said, reflect the Government's effort to make administrative provisions more sensitive to contemporary social realities.
Dr. Jitendra Singh said that the challenge before administration is not merely to frame rules and regulations but also to build strong institutions, nurture talent and create an ecosystem that is friendly and responsive to citizens.
The Minister said that today's administrators must be continuous learners, professionally competent, technology-savvy, ethically grounded and responsive to public expectations. Citizens increasingly assess the functioning of government through their everyday experiences, including the growing role of social media, making accountability and public responsiveness essential attributes of administration.
He placed particular emphasis on communication skills, describing them as especially important for administrators. He said civil servants must be equipped to communicate effectively with three important stakeholders: the general public, the media and elected representatives, including Ministers, Members of Parliament and Members of Legislative Assemblies.
Dr. Jitendra Singh said administrators must be able to engage constructively with citizens, including those raising grievances or participating in protests, while also maintaining effective communication with the media and responding appropriately to public representatives. He added that administrative training curricula must evolve accordingly, incorporating science, technology, communication and exposure to contemporary governance practices alongside traditional academic disciplines.
The Minister also invited State representatives to deliberate on personnel-related challenges, particularly central deputation and timely cadre reviews. He explained that central deputation provides officers with wider administrative exposure and professional opportunities, while also helping them remain prepared for changing responsibilities across different levels of government.
He said that delays in cadre reviews, sometimes extending over several years, can create administrative complications and affect career progression. States should therefore address such issues in a timely manner and develop constructive mechanisms to manage the administrative and institutional considerations involved.
The Minister also proposed reviving the concept of pairing States facing similar governance challenges to facilitate the exchange of solutions and successful practices.
Referring to technology-led administrative reforms, Dr. Jitendra Singh cited the Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS) and Digital Life Certificate initiatives as successful practices that have attracted international interest. He also referred to the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act and technology-driven examination procedures adopted by the Staff Selection Commission, where the elimination of unnecessary human interface has helped strengthen transparency and minimise the scope for malpractice.
The Minister further shared examples of employee-friendly workplace initiatives in Central Government offices, including gym facilities and crèches, and encouraged States to adopt suitable practices from the private sector to improve workplace efficiency and employee welfare.
Concluding his address, Dr. Jitendra Singh encouraged the participating officers to share their experiences, suggestions and State-specific challenges so that successful initiatives could be replicated and administrative bottlenecks addressed through collective deliberation. He said that sustained cooperation between the Centre and States, supported by innovation, institutional strengthening and citizen-centric governance, would be essential to building a more responsive and efficient public administration.

title: Two-day Power Ministers’ Conference begins in New Delhi
subtitle:
Rs 200 lakh Crore Investment Opportunity in the Power Sector in Next Two Decades

Demands Teamwork of all Stakeholders: Shri Manohar Lal
date:

content:
The two-day Power Ministers’ Conference commenced in New Delhi today. The conference (November 27-28, 2026) brings together Power Ministers, senior officials and electricity regulators from 28 States and 8 Union Territories and is chaired by Shri Manohar Lal, Union Minister of Power and Housing & Urban Affairs. The last such conference at the national level was held in 2024.
The Conference provides a platform for Centre–State deliberations on key policy priorities and implementation challenges in India’s power sector, with discussions focusing on strengthening energy security, improving power infrastructure and accelerating sectoral reforms.
While welcoming the participating State Power Ministers and other dignitaries, Shri Manohar Lal emphasised the need for the Centre and States to work together to develop the power sector. He said that India has made significant progress in expanding generation capacity, integrating renewable energy and strengthening the national grid. The next phase of our journey requires us to move towards a more integrated approach to power sector planning, where generation, storage, transmission and distribution are planned as interconnected elements of a single system. He stressed the necessity for States to implement Smart Meters, which offer significant benefits to consumers. The Minister also stated that, through collaboration with States and initiatives from the Ministry of Power, DISCOMS have achieved profitability after a prolonged period.
The Minister noted that the country’s power sector presents investment opportunity of Rs 200 lakh crores over the next two decades, and all stakeholders have to work together to make this possible. We have to work together with the private sector to ensure that we accomplish this, he said.
Shri Manohar Lal complimented the States and DISCOMs, as the DISCOMs as a whole turned a positive PAT during FY 2024-25. He said that we need to ensure that financial position of our DISCOMs is strengthened and necessary changes in policy, operations and regulation should facilitate the continuation of this turnaround.
While listing the main agenda of the Conference, he informed that Conference will comprise interactions and in-depth discussions among the Ministry of Power, States and other stakeholders on key issues such as implementation of Resource Adequacy (RA) plans, including accelerated energy storage deployment; inter-state and intra-state transmission issues; financial viability of Distribution Companies (DISCOMs); implementation of the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme (RDSS), with emphasis on smart metering, feeder separation and household electrification; and issues related to nuclear sites.
Shri Shripad Yesso Naik, Minister of State for Power in his address asked the participating States and UTs to share their experiences during the Conference, including difficulties in implementation, regulatory issues and areas where further support or intervention from the Central Government may be required. Our collective focus should be on moving from policy formulation to effective execution, from infrastructure creation to measurable outcomes, and from individual interventions to an integrated and sustainable power sector, the Minister said.
While addressing the participants, Shri Pankaj Agarwal, Secretary, Ministry of Power noted that the core guidance received from the Prime Minister is to move beyond energy security toward true energy independence in service of Viksit Bharat @ 2047. The past year has been one of record growth, he said, and noted that India’s installed capacity is now about 563 GW, and more than 55% of it is non-fossil. In the last 12 months around 60 GW of capacity was added, 87% of it from non-fossil sources, he said.
A key highlight on November 28 will be a joint session with the Forum of Regulators and State Electricity Regulatory Commissions (SERCs), bringing together State Power Ministers, SERC Chairpersons, State Secretaries for Power/Energy and Ministry officials to deliberate on issues concerning the power sector.
Senior officials from the Ministry of Power and representatives from participating States and Union Territories are also attending the Conference.

title: Breakthrough Achieved in 6.59 km Long Tunnel-14 of Rishikesh-Karnaprayag Rail Project
subtitle: Milestone Marks Significant Progress in Construction of the Strategically Important Rail Project in Uttarakhand
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                27 NOV 2026 5:12PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Indian Railways has achieved the main tunnel breakthrough of Tunnel-14, measuring 6.59 km, in the Rishikesh-Karnaprayag Rail Project today in Rudraprayag district of Uttarakhand. The breakthrough connects the two excavated sections of the tunnel, comprising 4.7 km from Portal-1 (Sumerpur) and 1.79 km from Portal-2 (Marora).
https://www.instagram.com/reel/DgPfP2Py2co/?evlk=bjFvYXRoMndsMXVy
At Portal-1 (T14P1), a 110-metre stretch of the triple-track tunnel was excavated through loose soil beneath inhabited areas, with 20-30 metres of soil and rock above it. Specialised techniques, including pre-excavation and multi-drifting, were used to ensure safe excavation.
At Portal-2 (T14P2), the slope was secured through 30–35-metre-deep micropiles, 15–20-metre-long rock bolts and consolidation grouting. These measures enabled the launch of the main tunnel drive in March 2024, following the resolution of ground settlement issues at Marora and matters related to land and home acquisition.
Approximately 100 metres of mechanical excavation was undertaken at Portal-2. To ensure the safety of nearby settlements, controlled blasting was carried out strictly during daytime hours near both portals.
Specialised ventilation systems were also deployed throughout the 4.7 km excavation drive from Portal-1 to ensure the supply of fresh air and regulate temperature inside the tunnel.
The breakthrough marks an important milestone in the construction of the Rishikesh–Karnaprayag Rail Project, an important railway infrastructure initiative aimed at improving rail connectivity in Uttarakhand. The project is expected to provide better connectivity to the hill regions, facilitate travel for pilgrims and tourists, and support regional development by improving accessibility to important destinations in the state.

title: NHAI Receives Overwhelming Response from Bidders for Construction of Ganga and Varuna Elevated Corridor Projects in Varanasi
subtitle: Total Four packages of the two projects received 32 bids for the elevated corridors along the Rivers Ganga and Varuna to ease congestion and improve urban connectivity
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                27 NOV 2026 6:02PM by PIB Delhi
content:
National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) has received an encouraging response from bidders for the development of two major elevated corridor projects along the Rivers Ganga and Varuna in Varanasi, that will help in decongesting the city and improve connectivity to key religious, cultural and transportation hubs. The two projects, with a combined length of around 89.2 km, will connect NH-31 and Varanasi Ring Road along the River Varuna; and NH-19 to Varanasi Ring Road along the River Ganga in Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh. The projects were approved by the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs in July 2026.
Both the projects will be implemented in two packages each. The Varuna Elevated Corridor received eight bids for Package-I and seven bids for Package-II. Similarly, the Ganga Elevated Corridor received eight bids for Package-I and nine bids for Package-II. Thus, all four packages together received a total of 32 bids, reflecting encouraging participation from the highway developers.
Varuna Elevated Corridor: Improved connectivity between NH-31 and Varanasi Ring Road
The 43.2 km long Varuna Elevated Corridor will connect NH-31 with the Varanasi Ring Road, running along River Varuna. The project will be implemented on Hybrid Annuity Model (HAM) with a total capital cost of Rs.10,998.32 crore and will provide improved access to important transport terminals as well as key locations in Varanasi city. The project comprises a 6/4-lane predominantly elevated corridor, including main carriageway, flyovers, loops, ramps, service roads and will be implemented in two packages.
The corridor is a major component of the Varanasi Decongestion Plan and will provide seamless connectivity between NH-31 and Kashi Railway Station, while substantially improving access to Varanasi Ring Road, Varanasi Airport, Kashi Railway Station, Varanasi City Railway Station, Varanasi Junction, Deen Dayal Upadhyaya Junction, Ramnagar Port, Sampurnanand Sanskrit University, the ghats of Varanasi and the adjoining Chandauli region.
Designed for an operating speed of 80–100 km/h, the project will reduce travel time between NH-31 and Kashi Railway Station from approximately 40 minutes to 20 minutes, representing a reduction of nearly 50 per cent. It will significantly decongest the city’s road network, improve road safety, reduce vehicle operating costs and facilitate faster, uninterrupted movement of passenger and freight traffic.
The project will also strengthen regional connectivity by improving access to one Economic Node (Chandauli Social Economic Zone), one Social Node (Chandauli) and six major Logistics Nodes, thereby enhancing multimodal integration in line with the PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan. It will facilitate efficient movement of agricultural produce, industrial goods, construction materials and minerals, improve logistics efficiency and supporting sustainable economic growth across eastern Uttar Pradesh.
Ganga Elevated Corridor: Strengthening riverfront connectivity and access to key destinations
The 46 km long six lane elevated Ganga Corridor will connect NH-19 with Varanasi Ring Road, providing riverbank connectivity along the River Ganga. The project will be implemented on Hybrid Annuity Model (HAM) at a total capital cost of Rs.14,447.64 crore. The project has been divided into two packages and includes construction of a six-lane elevated main carriageway, a 910-meter-long cable-stayed bridge, a 1.32 km long extradosed Foot Over Bridge-cum-Major Bridge, loops, ramps, link roads and service roads.
The corridor has been conceived as a transformative urban mobility project to decongest the road network of Varanasi & Chandauli by providing a high-speed, access-controlled connection between NH-19, the Varanasi Ring Road (NH-135B), Ramnagar/ BHU and other major urban destinations. Designed for an operating speed of 80–100 km/h, it will reduce average travel time from around 60 minutes to 20 minutes, representing a reduction of nearly 67 per cent. Travel time between NH-19 and Kashi Railway Station will be reduced from approximately 50 minutes to about 25 minutes, resulting in a saving of about 25 minutes (nearly 50 per cent).
Aligned with the PM Gati Shakti National Master Plan, the corridor will strengthen multimodal connectivity by providing seamless access to major highways, railway stations, Lal Bahadur Shastri Airport and Ramnagar IWAI Port, while significantly improving connectivity to key religious, educational and cultural landmarks, including the Kashi Vishwanath Temple, Banaras Hindu University (BHU), Namo Ghat, Ramnagar Fort and the Ghats of Varanasi. By linking important economic, social and logistics nodes, the project will improve logistics efficiency, enhance road safety, facilitate tourism and pilgrimage, and support sustainable regional economic growth across eastern Uttar Pradesh.
Both these elevated corridor projects are aimed at addressing growing traffic requirements of Varanasi city. By providing improved connectivity between the National Highways, ring road and important city destinations, the projects will help to reduce traffic congestion in the urban centre, facilitate smoother movement of local and through traffic and improve accessibility for residents, commuters and pilgrims. The projects will also support tourism and pilgrimage-related activities, stimulate economic growth and contribute to the socio-economic development of Varanasi and surrounding region.

title: Dr. Jitendra Singh Inaugurates BSL-3 Facility at CSIR-CDRI Lucknow; Says India Moving Towards Becoming a Global Hub for Innovative Drug Discovery and Development
subtitle:
New BSL-3/ABSL-3 Facility at CSIR-CDRI Lucknow to Strengthen India's Research Capabilities Against Challenging Infectious Diseases: Dr. Jitendra Singh

CDRI Has Developed 13 Drugs That Have Reached the Market, Licensed Over 80 Process Technologies and Filed More Than 1,000 Patents: Dr. Jitendra Singh

India's Pharmaceutical Sector Must Move Beyond Generic Drug Manufacturing to Become a Global Discoverer of Innovative Medicines: Dr. Jitendra Singh

Minister Emphasises Industry Partnerships, Artificial Intelligence and Clinical Translation to Accelerate Drug Discovery and Advance Viksit Bharat 2047
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                27 NOV 2026 5:26PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science and Technology and Vice President, CSIR, Dr. Jitendra Singh today inaugurated the state-of-the-art Biosafety Level-3 (BSL-3)/Animal Biosafety Level-3 (ABSL-3) Facility and Dr. B. Mukerji Lecture Theatre at CSIR-Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI), Lucknow, and hailed India’s health innovations saying that India is moving towards becoming a global hub for innovative drug discovery and development.
The Minister said that the country must now move beyond its established position as a major global supplier of generic medicines and emerge as a discoverer and developer of innovative therapeutics, with indigenous research, clinical development and industry partnerships playing a critical role in this transition. This shift, he said, is essential for strengthening India’s pharmaceutical leadership and achieving the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047.
The programme was attended by Dr. Radha Rangarajan, Director, CSIR-CDRI; Dr. Prabodh K. Trivedi, Director, CSIR-CIMAP; former Director of CSIR-CDRI Dr. Madhu Dikshit; representatives of ICMR–National Institute of Research in Tribal Health, Jabalpur; Uttar Pradesh University of Medical Sciences, Saifai; and Medanta Hospital, Lucknow, besides scientists, researchers, students, technical and non-technical staff and industry representatives.
The newly inaugurated BSL-3/ABSL-3 facility will provide high-containment research infrastructure for scientific studies involving Mycobacterium tuberculosis and non-tuberculous mycobacteria (NTM), strengthening the Institute’s capabilities in research on challenging infectious diseases. Dr. Jitendra Singh also congratulated CSIR-CDRI on the collaborative agreements signed with ICMR–National Institute of Research in Tribal Health, Uttar Pradesh University of Medical Sciences and Medanta Hospital, expressing confidence that these partnerships would lead to fruitful collaborative research programmes, accelerate clinical translation and deliver measurable benefits to society.
The Minister said that under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, science, technology and innovation have become central to India’s national development, with a strong emphasis on research that addresses citizens’ needs and delivers tangible solutions. He cited CSIR-CDRI’s journey from drug discovery and clinical development to diagnostics, process technologies and affordable healthcare interventions as an example of how scientific research can translate into meaningful public benefit.
CSIR-CDRI has developed 13 drugs that have reached the market, licensed more than 80 process technologies and six diagnostic technologies, published over 12,000 research articles and filed more than 456 international patents and 586 patents in India. Its research infrastructure includes a compound library of approximately 90,000 molecules, more than 50 animal models and over 30 in-vitro screening systems, alongside advanced analytical instrumentation, GLP-certified toxicology and safety pharmacology facilities and specialised cardiac safety assessment infrastructure.
Referring to CDRI’s contribution to public healthcare, Dr. Jitendra Singh cited Centchroman, also known as Ormeloxifene, an indigenous non-steroidal, once-a-week oral contraceptive developed by the Institute. Its inclusion in the National Family Planning Programme in 2016 marked an important milestone in translating indigenous scientific research into a public health intervention. More than 350 lakh strips have been distributed free of cost to women across the country through ASHA workers during the last five years, with the current user base exceeding five lakh women.
The Minister also referred to CDRI’s promising drug-development pipeline, including a standardised extract of Picrorhiza kurroa for non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, now referred to as metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), which has completed Phase III clinical trials. Two other compounds discovered at CDRI, L-Ormeloxifene for contraception and S007-1500 for fracture healing, have entered Phase I clinical trials. The Institute is also pursuing advanced research leads for malaria, cancer, neuropathic pain and age-related macular degeneration, along with phytopharmaceutical candidates for cancer and Parkinson’s disease.
Dr. Jitendra Singh said India ranks third globally in pharmaceutical production by volume and 11th by value and is among the world’s largest suppliers of generic medicines, meeting over 50 per cent of Africa’s generic medicine requirements and approximately 40 per cent of the generic drug demand in the United States. While appreciating the achievements of India’s pharmaceutical industry, he said the next phase of growth must involve moving up the value chain, from predominantly manufacturing generic medicines to discovering and developing innovative therapeutics.
He said drug discovery and development are complex, expensive and high-risk endeavours requiring sustained investment and long-term commitment. National research institutions must pursue cutting-edge science, explore novel targets and mechanisms and generate robust proof-of-concept data, while pharmaceutical companies should be encouraged to take promising discoveries forward through further development, clinical evaluation and commercialisation. Stronger technology-transfer mechanisms and early industry participation can create an effective pathway from laboratory research to patients.
Appreciating CDRI’s ongoing collaborations with Zydus, Cipla, Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories, Himalaya, Themis Medicare and several startups, the Minister encouraged the Institute to further strengthen its role as a research and innovation partner for the pharmaceutical industry.
Calling for greater adoption of emerging technologies, Dr. Jitendra Singh said the integration of biology, chemistry, computational sciences and artificial intelligence offers tremendous opportunities to transform drug discovery. He encouraged scientists to pursue ambitious research questions, embrace out-of-the-box ideas and work closely with clinicians, hospitals and industry partners to ensure that research remains aligned with actual clinical requirements. At every stage of drug discovery and development, the ultimate beneficiary must be the patient, he said.
The Minister also appreciated CDRI’s contribution to scientific capacity building, with the Institute having trained more than 2,000 PhDs and over 10,000 trainees. He said skilled researchers, technologists and regulatory specialists are indispensable to a strong innovation ecosystem and that the contribution of CDRI-trained professionals across academia, startups, industry and research organisations represents a valuable national investment.
Dr. Jitendra Singh expressed confidence that CSIR-CDRI would continue to strengthen India’s capabilities in indigenous drug discovery and contribute significantly to the national vision of Viksit Bharat 2047. Quoting former President Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, he said, “Dream, dream, dream. Dreams transform into thoughts and thoughts result in action.” He encouraged the scientific community to dream big, translate scientific ideas into discoveries and develop medicines that improve and save lives.
